questions.title: Which of the following does NOT describe the anatomical position?
questions.question: All of the following describe the standard anatomical position EXCEPT:

options.A: Standing erect with the eyes looking forward
options.B: Upper limbs hanging at the sides with the palms facing forward
options.C: Lower limbs together with the feet pointing forward
options.D: Forearms flexed at the elbow with the palms facing the trunk

explanations.D: Correct. The anatomical position holds the upper limb fully extended at the elbow and hanging by the side with the palm rotated to face forward (fully supinated), not flexed at the elbow with the palm turned toward the trunk. Every anatomical description — every 'superior', 'anterior', 'medial' — is written as if the body stands in this one fixed reference posture, which is exactly why its criteria are fixed rather than left to whatever position a patient happens to be lying in. A flexed elbow with the palm facing the trunk is the forearm's default resting (pronated) posture, and anatomical position specifically corrects for that default by extending the elbow and supinating the forearm so both sides of the body can be described symmetrically.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Standing erect with the eyes looking forward (the head level, gaze directed to the horizon) is one of the defining criteria of anatomical position.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper limbs hanging at the sides with the palms facing forward is a defining criterion of anatomical position, not an exception to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lower limbs together with the feet pointing forward is a defining criterion of anatomical position, not an exception to it.

questions.learning_objective: State the criteria that define the standard anatomical position, and recognise a flexed, pronated forearm as inconsistent with it.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} (anatomical-position criteria item, keyed).

field_notes.au: Q6 of the Nebras dept bank asks which statement is true of anatomical position; this record tests the same criteria set from the opposite (EXCEPT) direction.

questions.title: Which anatomical plane divides the body into upper and lower parts?
questions.question: Which anatomical plane divides the body into upper and lower parts?

explanations.C: Correct. The transverse (horizontal) plane runs at right angles to the body's long axis, and of the three cardinal anatomical planes it is the one that leaves an upper (superior) part and a lower (inferior) part behind. The sagittal plane instead cuts along the long axis to leave a right and a left part, and the coronal plane cuts along the long axis the other way to leave a front (anterior) and a back (posterior) part. Naming each plane by the two parts it leaves behind — transverse leaves upper and lower — is the quickest way to keep the three from being confused under exam pressure, since 'oblique' names no fixed pair of parts at all.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The sagittal (median) plane divides the body into right and left parts, not upper and lower.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The coronal (frontal) plane divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts, not upper and lower.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An oblique plane is any plane not aligned with the three cardinal planes; it is not one of the three named planes and defines no fixed pair of parts.

questions.learning_objective: Name the transverse plane as the one that divides the body into upper and lower parts, and distinguish it from the sagittal and coronal planes.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} (Q4, plane dividing superior/inferior, keyed C).

questions.title: Which pair of terms describes distance from the root of a limb?
questions.question: Which pair of terms of position is used to describe how far a point lies from the root of a limb?

explanations.C: Correct. Proximal and distal measure distance from the root of a limb — proximal nearer the trunk, distal further from it — and are the terms of position used whenever two structures along a limb's own long axis are compared, for example describing the plantar surface as more distal than a point on the leg. Medial and lateral instead measure distance from the median plane, not from a limb's root, so the two pairs answer different questions even though both are called terms of position. Keeping the reference point straight — the median plane for medial/lateral, the limb's own root for proximal/distal — is the exact distinction the department book's terms-of-position items are built to test.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Medial and lateral measure distance from the median plane, not from the root of a limb.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Superior and inferior measure position along the body's vertical (up/down) axis, not distance from a limb's root.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superficial and deep measure distance from the body's surface, not distance from a limb's root.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish proximal/distal (referenced to a limb's root) from medial/lateral (referenced to the median plane).
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} (terms-of-position item on the plantar surface of the foot, keyed).

questions.title: Which bone belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
questions.question: Which of the following bones is part of the appendicular skeleton?

explanations.C: Correct. The humerus is a bone of the upper limb, and the limbs together with their girdles (pectoral and pelvic) make up the appendicular skeleton — the part of the skeleton attached to, rather than forming, the body's central axis. The axial skeleton, by contrast, is the skull, hyoid, sternum, ribs and vertebral column: the central bony frame the limbs hang from. Sorting a bone correctly into axial or appendicular is the single most-tested classification in this chapter, precisely because a few bones (the pectoral and pelvic girdles) sit at the join between the two and are easy to place wrongly.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The sternum is part of the axial skeleton.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The skull is part of the axial skeleton.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ribs are part of the axial skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: Classify the humerus as appendicular and the sternum, skull and ribs as axial.

questions.title: What is the largest sesamoid bone in the body?
questions.question: Which of the following is the largest sesamoid bone in the body?

explanations.A: Correct. The patella develops within the tendon of quadriceps femoris and is the largest of the body's sesamoid bones — one of the six shape classes bones fall into, alongside long, short, flat, irregular and pneumatic bones, each with its own worked example in the department book. A sesamoid bone forms inside a tendon where it crosses a joint under high compressive load, protecting the tendon and improving its mechanical leverage, and the patella is the clearest illustration of both roles at once, sitting over the knee. Smaller sesamoid bones exist elsewhere (for example at the base of the thumb), but none rivals the patella in size.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pisiform is a genuine carpal (wrist) bone, not a sesamoid bone, despite its small rounded shape.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sacrum is an irregular bone formed by the fusion of five vertebrae, not a sesamoid bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The scaphoid is a carpal (wrist) bone, not a sesamoid bone.

questions.learning_objective: Name the patella as the largest sesamoid bone, and place sesamoid bones among the six shape classes.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras / Questions Anatomy (twin banks), largest sesamoid bone item, keyed.

questions.title: Which is NOT a function of a pneumatic bone's air cavities?
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the air cavities in a pneumatic bone?

options.A: Lightening the weight of the skull

explanations.D: Correct. The air-filled cavities of a pneumatic bone do the opposite of adding strength: any mechanical strength the skull's pneumatic bones retain comes from their outer compact-bone shell, not from the air spaces themselves, which exist despite reducing the bone's mass rather than because they reinforce it. What the cavities buy the body instead is a lighter skull, a resonating chamber that gives the voice its individual quality, and a lining surface that warms and humidifies inspired air on its way to the lungs. A bone that needed maximum mechanical strength — a weight-bearing long bone, for instance — is never built pneumatic, which is itself evidence that air cavities and strength trade against, rather than reinforce, one another.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Lightening the skull is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giving the voice its resonance is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Warming inspired air is one of the genuine functions of pneumatic bone air cavities.

questions.learning_objective: State the three genuine functions of a pneumatic bone's air cavities, and recognise that added mechanical strength is not one of them.

questions.title: What separates the epiphysis from the diaphysis of a growing long bone?
questions.question: What separates the epiphysis from the diaphysis of a growing long bone?

explanations.B: Correct. A long bone is an epiphysis at each end, a diaphysis (shaft) between them, and a metaphysis where the two meet — and while the bone is still growing, the epiphysis and diaphysis are separated at that junction by a layer of epiphyseal (growth-plate) cartilage rather than being continuous bone. This cartilage plate is where the shaft actually lengthens, by cartilage cells proliferating and then being replaced by bone on the diaphyseal side, until it finally ossifies once growth is complete and the epiphysis fuses to the shaft. Until that fusion, an X-ray of a growing long bone shows a visible radiolucent line at exactly this epiphysis-diaphysis boundary, which is the growth plate the question is naming.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The periosteum is the fibrous covering on the outer surface of the whole bone; it does not separate the epiphysis from the diaphysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The medullary cavity is the marrow-containing space inside the diaphysis; it does not sit at the epiphysis-diaphysis junction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Articular cartilage covers the joint surface at the end of the epiphysis; it does not separate the epiphysis from the diaphysis.

questions.learning_objective: Name the epiphyseal (growth) cartilage as the structure separating the epiphysis from the diaphysis in a growing long bone.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras / Questions Anatomy (twin banks), epiphysis/diaphysis separator item, keyed.

questions.title: Which long bone has its growing end at its upper extremity?
questions.question: Which of the following long bones has its growing end (the end that ossifies later) at its upper extremity?

explanations.D: Correct. The humerus's growing end — the end whose epiphyseal plate ossifies later and therefore contributes more to the bone's final length — is at its upper (proximal, shoulder) end, unlike the radius and ulna, whose growing end is at their lower (distal, wrist) end. This is the single most-repeated Anatomy fact in this module's exam corpus, appearing across both EOM paper pairs, precisely because the growing-end rule flips direction between the upper and lower limb: upper-limb long bones grow away from the elbow, while lower-limb long bones grow towards the knee. The femur (lower end) and tibia (upper end) follow the lower-limb half of that same rule, which is exactly why they are the two distractors most likely to be confused with the humerus here.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The femur's growing end is at its lower (distal, knee) end, not its upper end.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tibia's growing end is at its upper (proximal, knee) end, but the tibia is a lower-limb bone following the opposite half of the same rule, not the humerus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The radius's growing end is at its lower (distal, wrist) end, not its upper end.

questions.learning_objective: Name the humerus's upper end as its growing end, and state that upper-limb long bones grow away from the elbow while lower-limb long bones grow towards the knee.

questions.title: Which direction does a long bone's nutrient artery run?
questions.question: The nutrient artery of a long bone runs obliquely through the shaft towards which end?

options.C: Directly transverse to the long axis of the shaft
options.D: Parallel to the periosteal arteries, along the outer surface

explanations.B: Correct. A long bone takes four sets of arteries, and the shaft's own supply is divided between two of them: the nutrient artery runs inside the shaft, entering through the nutrient foramen and slanting obliquely away from the growing end towards the non-growing end, while periosteal arteries supply the shaft from the outer surface instead. This oblique, fixed direction is a reliable radiological landmark — the nutrient canal on an X-ray points towards the end of the bone that ossifies earlier (fuses first), which is the opposite end from wherever the bone's own growing end happens to be. The remaining two of the four arterial sets, epiphyseal and metaphyseal arteries, supply the two ends of the bone separately from this shaft supply.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The nutrient artery runs away from the growing end, not towards it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nutrient artery runs obliquely along the shaft, not transverse to its long axis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nutrient artery runs inside the shaft (through the nutrient foramen and canal), while the periosteal arteries are the ones on the outer surface — the two are a different pair of the bone's four arterial sets, not the same vessel described twice.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nutrient artery runs obliquely towards a long bone's non-growing end, and place it among the bone's four arterial sets.

questions.title: A bone forming directly within a connective tissue membrane is undergoing which type of ossification?
questions.question: A bone that forms directly within a connective tissue membrane, without first passing through a cartilage stage, is undergoing which type of ossification?

explanations.B: Correct. A bone forms either directly within a connective tissue membrane (membranous, or intramembranous, ossification) or by first laying down a cartilage model and then replacing it with bone (endochondral, or intracartilaginous, ossification), and which route it takes is fixed for each individual bone rather than a matter of stage or age. The flat bones of the skull vault and the clavicle are the department's own worked examples of membranous ossification, while the long bones are the worked example of the endochondral route, forming first as a cartilage template that a primary centre, and later a secondary centre, progressively replace with bone. Because the route is fixed per bone, a skull bone never switches to the cartilage route partway through development, and a long bone never switches to the membrane route — each bone commits to one mechanism from the start.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Endochondral ossification replaces a pre-existing cartilage model with bone; it is not direct membrane-to-bone formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Appositional growth is how a bone increases in width or thickness by adding new bone at its outer surface; it is not one of the two named routes by which a bone first ossifies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Metaplastic ossification' is not one of the two named routes of ossification taught in this chapter.

questions.learning_objective: Name membranous ossification as direct membrane-to-bone formation, and endochondral ossification as replacement of a cartilage model, and give the department's own worked example of each.

questions.title: Which joint is a hinge (uniaxial) synovial joint?
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a hinge (uniaxial) synovial joint?

explanations.B: Correct. Each joint of the upper limb is classified by the shape of its articular surfaces, and no two neighbouring joints share a type - the elbow's articular surfaces are shaped so that movement is possible around only one axis, making it a uniaxial hinge joint permitting flexion and extension alone. The shoulder and hip, by contrast, are ball-and-socket joints, whose spherical articular surfaces allow movement around three axes (flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and rotation, combining into circumduction). The wrist's articular surfaces instead give it an ellipsoid (condylar) shape, allowing movement around two axes rather than one, which is why it can flex, extend, abduct and adduct but not rotate on its own.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, allowing movement around three axes, not a uniaxial hinge joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, allowing movement around three axes, not a uniaxial hinge joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The wrist is an ellipsoid (condylar) joint, allowing movement around two axes, not a uniaxial hinge joint.

questions.learning_objective: Name the elbow as a uniaxial hinge joint, and distinguish it from the ball-and-socket shoulder/hip and the ellipsoid wrist.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} (hinge-joint-locations item, keyed).

field_notes.au: The Foundation module tests joint-by-axis classification generically rather than only through 101-ISK's own upper-limb-specific worked examples; this record uses the elbow as its worked example, matching the department bank's own hinge-joint item.

questions.title: A pivot joint permits movement around how many axes?
questions.question: A pivot joint permits movement around how many axes?

options.D: The number of axes is not fixed for this joint type

explanations.A: Correct. The movements possible at a joint follow directly from its type and the number of its axes, and a pivot joint is uniaxial: its articular surfaces let one bone rotate around a single fixed axis relative to the other, as at the proximal radioulnar joint (pronation/supination) or the atlanto-axial joint (rotation of the head). This is the same one-axis restriction a hinge joint has, but the movement each permits is different - a hinge flexes and extends around its single axis, a pivot rotates around it - which is why 'uniaxial' alone does not fully describe a joint without also naming its shape. Joints with more axes allow correspondingly more movement types: two axes (condylar/ellipsoid) add a second plane of movement, and three axes (ball-and-socket) add rotation on top of both, which is exactly the axis-count logic this chapter's items are testing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two axes describes a condylar or ellipsoid joint, not a pivot joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Three axes describes a ball-and-socket joint, not a pivot joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The number of axes at a synovial joint is fixed by its shape, not variable - a pivot joint is always uniaxial.

questions.learning_objective: State that a pivot joint is uniaxial, and that the movements available at any synovial joint follow from its type and axis count.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} ('pivot joint considers a... uniaxial' item, keyed).

questions.title: Which nerve does NOT supply the elbow joint?
questions.question: Which of the following nerves does NOT contribute a branch to the nerve supply of the elbow joint?

explanations.D: Correct. The elbow takes twigs from four nerves that cross it - the musculocutaneous, radial, median and ulnar nerves - and the axillary nerve is not one of them, since the axillary nerve's own territory is the shoulder region (deltoid and teres minor, plus the overlying skin), well proximal to the elbow. This pattern follows Hilton's law: the nerve supply of a joint is provided by the nerves that supply the muscles acting on it, and each of the four elbow nerves supplies at least one muscle crossing the joint (for example the musculocutaneous nerve supplies brachialis, a flexor of the elbow). The axillary nerve supplies no muscle acting on the elbow, which is exactly why Hilton's law predicts it plays no part in the elbow's own nerve supply.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve is one of the four nerves supplying the elbow joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial nerve is one of the four nerves supplying the elbow joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median nerve is one of the four nerves supplying the elbow joint.

questions.learning_objective: Name the four nerves supplying the elbow joint (musculocutaneous, radial, median, ulnar), identify the axillary nerve as the exception, and connect the pattern to Hilton's law.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras, p.{page} (Hilton's law general-principle item, keyed).

questions.title: Which type of muscle lines the wall of the alimentary canal?
questions.question: Which type of muscle lines the wall of the alimentary canal?

explanations.C: Correct. The three muscle types are told apart by four things at once - where they are, whether they are voluntary, whether they are striated, and which nerves supply them - and smooth muscle is the type that is involuntary, non-striated, supplied by the autonomic nervous system, and found in the walls of hollow viscera including the alimentary canal from oesophagus to rectum. This lets smooth muscle contract in the slow, sustained, involuntary waves (peristalsis) that move food along the gut without any conscious control being possible or necessary. Skeletal muscle, by contrast, is voluntary and striated and moves the skeleton, while cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated and is confined to the heart wall - neither fits the alimentary canal's own requirement for sustained involuntary contraction.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated, and moves the skeleton, not the wall of the alimentary canal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and striated, but is confined to the wall of the heart, not the alimentary canal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 'Striated voluntary muscle' describes skeletal muscle, which is not the type found in the alimentary canal's wall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify smooth muscle as involuntary, non-striated and autonomically supplied, and name it as the type lining the alimentary canal.
questions.source_citation: Alexandria University AU-MED-102 Anatomy department bank, MCQs - Foundation Anatomy & Embryology mcqs Nebras / Questions Anatomy (twin banks), alimentary-canal-muscle-type item, keyed.

questions.title: A flat, sheet-like connective tissue attachment of a muscle to bone is called a(n):
questions.question: A muscle that attaches to bone via a flat, sheet-like layer of connective tissue, rather than a cord-like structure, is attached by a(n):

explanations.B: Correct. A muscle attaches either directly to bone, or through a tendon, or through an aponeurosis - a flat, sheet-like band of connective tissue that spreads a muscle's pull over a broad attachment rather than concentrating it at a single cord-like point. The external oblique's attachment to the linea alba, and the epicranial aponeurosis connecting the frontalis and occipitalis muscles across the scalp, are classic worked examples of this sheet-like attachment. A tendon, by contrast, is the cord-like route for the same job, transmitting a muscle's pull to a narrow, concentrated point on bone rather than spreading it across a broad sheet.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A tendon is the cord-like, not sheet-like, route by which a muscle attaches to bone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A ligament connects bone to bone, not muscle to bone, so it is not one of the ways a muscle itself attaches.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A raphe is a fibrous line where two muscles meet each other in the midline (for example the pharyngeal raphe), not a muscle-to-bone attachment.

questions.learning_objective: Name the aponeurosis as the flat, sheet-like route by which a muscle attaches to bone, and distinguish it from a tendon, a ligament and a raphe.

questions.title: In elbow extension, triceps brachii acts as the:
questions.question: In elbow extension, triceps brachii acts as the:

explanations.D: Correct. A purposeful movement needs four kinds of muscle, each named for what it does to the movement rather than for where it lies, and the prime mover (or agonist) is the muscle that directly produces the movement in question - triceps brachii is the prime mover of elbow extension because its contraction is what straightens the joint. The other three roles describe different jobs in the same movement: the antagonist (biceps brachii, here) relaxes in a controlled way to allow the movement; a fixator stabilises a nearby joint (for example the shoulder) so the prime mover has a stable base to pull from; and a synergist prevents an unwanted action at an intermediate joint that the prime mover would otherwise also produce. Naming triceps as the prime mover, specifically, rather than as any of the other three roles, is the exact distinction this item is testing.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The antagonist for elbow extension is biceps brachii, which relaxes to allow the movement - triceps is not acting as an antagonist here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A fixator stabilises a nearby joint so the prime mover can act; triceps is itself producing the movement, not stabilising a neighbouring joint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A synergist prevents an unwanted action at an intermediate joint; triceps is the muscle directly producing elbow extension, not a synergist to it.

questions.learning_objective: Name triceps brachii as the prime mover of elbow extension, and distinguish prime mover from antagonist, fixator and synergist.

questions.title: Lymph from the right lower limb drains into which of the following?
questions.question: Lymph from the right lower limb drains into which of the following?

options.C: Cisterna chyli, with no further drainage beyond it
options.D: The left subclavian vein directly, bypassing any lymphatic duct

explanations.B: Correct. The right lymphatic duct drains one quadrant of the body - the right side of the head and neck, the right upper limb, and the right side of the thorax - while the thoracic duct drains the other three-quarters, including both lower limbs, so lymph from the right lower limb reaches the venous system via the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct. The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli in the abdomen, ascends through the thorax, and empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins, so the cisterna chyli is a way-station on this route rather than lymph's final destination. This asymmetric split - one small duct for one quadrant, one large duct for the other three - is the single fact the EOM paper's own item on the thoracic duct is built to test.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head/neck, the right upper limb, and the right thorax - not the right lower limb.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cisterna chyli is a dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct, not the endpoint of lymph drainage; lymph continues from it through the thoracic duct to the venous system.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lymph from the right lower limb reaches the venous system via the thoracic duct, which empties into the venous system at the left subclavian/internal jugular junction - it does not bypass the duct.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct, drains the right lower limb, and name the thoracic duct's own venous termination.

questions.title: Which fibre arrangement gives skeletal muscle the greatest range of movement?
questions.question: Which pattern of skeletal muscle fibre arrangement gives the greatest range of movement?

explanations.C: Correct. Skeletal muscles are classified by the direction of their fibres, from strap-like (parallel) to multipennate, and parallel fibres run the full length of the muscle in line with its long axis, so the muscle as a whole can shorten by roughly the same proportion each individual fibre shortens - giving parallel muscles the widest range of movement of any fibre arrangement. Pennate muscles (unipennate, bipennate and multipennate) instead angle their shorter fibres obliquely onto a central tendon, which packs in more fibres for a given muscle volume and so generates more force, but at the cost of each fibre contributing less to the muscle's overall length change. This is a genuine trade-off, not a simple hierarchy: parallel architecture is built for range of movement, and increasingly pennate architecture is built for increasing force, which is exactly why the exam item asks for the widest range specifically rather than the strongest muscle.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Unipennate fibres angle onto one side of a central tendon, trading range of movement for force - the opposite of the widest-range answer this item asks for.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multipennate fibres angle onto a central tendon from multiple directions, giving the greatest force of the listed arrangements but the least range of movement, not the greatest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bipennate fibres angle onto both sides of a central tendon, trading range of movement for force, like the other pennate arrangements.

questions.learning_objective: Name parallel (strap-like) fibre architecture as giving the widest range of movement, and pennate architecture as trading range for force.
